preamble: In Portuguese the word-final nasal vowel [ã] of Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin -anem, developed a labial off-glide and became the nasal diphthong [ɐ̃w̃], spelled ⟨ão⟩: can (also cã) 'dog' > cão, pan (also pã) 'bread' > pão. Galician, which kept the forms can and pan, shows no diphthong, so the change belongs to Portuguese alone.

examples.from: Old Galician-Portuguese can /ˈkã/ (also cã) 'dog', from Latin canem
examples.note: [ɐ̃w̃] is a nasalized [au]-type diphthong, filed under atlas au (no nasal-diphthong cell).

examples.from: Old Galician-Portuguese pan (also pã) 'bread', from Latin pānem
examples.note: Galician keeps can and pan without the diphthong.
